#6060. New York JFK Terminal 6 Is Almost Open: Airlines & Lounges Moving In

New York Kennedy Airport (JFK) is currently undergoing a $19 billion modernization. While this includes all kinds of updates, the two biggest developments are the opening of two new terminals — we’re talking about Terminal 6 and Terminal One (not to be confused with Terminal 1).

As you’d expect, the opening of both terminals has been delayed, since airport construction rarely runs on time. Per the latest updates, the expectation is that Terminal 6 will open before the end of 2026, while Terminal One will open in the first quarter of 2027.

Along those lines, it’s looking like we might just be days away from the opening of Terminal 6, so I’d like to cover all the details we know.

JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open with a phased approach as of December 2026. To cover the very basics:

The below video of the terminal should give you a good sense of what to expect in terms of the passenger experience, so I’d recommend checking that out.

All things considered, this new terminal moving is awesome, given the quality of terminals at JFK otherwise. For those originating or terminating in New York, this should be ideal. For those connecting to or from JetBlue in Terminal 5, this will also make connections much easier. Meanwhile for a limited number of other passengers, this might make connections a bit more complicated, for cases where airlines are moving away from their partners (like Cathay Pacific moving from American’s Terminal 8 to Terminal 6).

Roughly 17 airlines are expected to eventually operate out of JFK Terminal 6, though that will happen in two phases. Broadly speaking, we’ll see some JetBlue operations move there (since the airline is a core tenant), and on top of that, we’ll largely see airlines move from Terminal 1, Terminal 7, and Terminal 8.

So the expectation is that the following airlines will eventually operate from JFK Terminal 6:

There is still a bit of a mystery as to the order in which airlines will move to JFK Terminal 6. For one, there’s the two phases of the terminal opening, but even within each phase, it won’t fully be overnight.

We know that All Nippon Airways, Cathay Pacific, Condor, Frontier, Lufthansa Group carriers, and TAP Air Portugal, will move in the first phase. Meanwhile we know that Air India will move in the second phase. But for the remainder of the airlines, there’s a lack of certainty on that front.

Now, we’ll see if this sticks, and how accurate it is, but current schedule filings suggest that Condor will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 3, while Cathay Pacific will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 15 (thanks to Peter_ for flagging this). So it sounds like we could potentially be just over a week from the first airline moving, which would be awesome!

In terms of lounges, we have confirmation that Terminal 6 will have outposts from Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, Aer Lingus, and Air India. Hopefully the new lounges are ready to go as airlines make the move, but I wouldn’t consider that to be a sure thing, given the complexity of airport operations.

The Air India lounge definitely won’t open anytime soon, since the airline is only moving in the second phase. Meanwhile the Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, and Aer Lingus lounges, will hopefully open soon(ish). Of course I’m most excited to see what Cathay Pacific has in store, given its amazing lounge quality.

JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open before the end of 2026, and if current filings are to be believed, the move could happen as soon as early December. It appears that Condor and Cathay Pacific might be among the first airlines to move, so hopefully Cathay Pacific’s new lounge isn’t too far behind. So we’ll mark this as “developing,” but the completion of the first exciting phase of this $19 billion project is imminent.

Are you excited for the new JFK Terminal 6?

@John agreed, it looks tight on paper. My guess is the evening Europe bank will lean on remote stands and the T5 connection early on. This seems like an awful lot of carriers for so few gates, no? Just off the top of my head, I recall that Aer Lingus (Dublin + Shannon), Lufthansa (Frankfurt + Munich), SWISS (Zurich + Geneva) and TAP (Lisbon + Porto) operate *multiple* daily frequencies to JFK. When you pair these European carriers with Austrian, Brussels, Condor and Norse, I would think the transatlantic slot times in particular (eg, 5-9pm) would quickly result in too many planes for too few gates. I’m sure this has been considered but this seems poorly planned, at least on the surface.

#6059. Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

“The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

At issue is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”

The letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

Advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly said it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the issue.

Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they plan to bring up a vote next year.

Senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

“Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump said, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

Trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

“Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most important stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”

The House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the issue.

“Across the political spectrum,” the letter said, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to new national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”

There is a lot to love about JetBlue. The airline offers generous legroom, tasty snacks and free Wi-Fi. It also has a fairly straightforward loyalty program.

JetBlue TrueBlue points are easy to earn through flights, partner activity, cobranded credit cards and transferable rewards. They are also easy to redeem because any seat on a JetBlue-operated flight can be booked with points, and there are no blackout dates. The program has become more useful through an expanding network of airline partners, including the Blue Sky partnership with United Airlines.

Here is everything you need to know about the JetBlue TrueBlue loyalty program.

JetBlue serves more than 100 destinations throughout the U.S., Latin America, Canada, the Caribbean and Europe. The airline isn’t part of any global alliance but has a growing roster of airline partners.

With JetBlue being one of the youngest major airlines in the U.S., the TrueBlue loyalty program is a relative newcomer to the points and miles world. The program is revenue-based, so earning and redeeming points are typically tied to ticket prices. However, there are also many ways to earn JetBlue points without even getting on an airplane.

TrueBlue points do not expire. Points Pooling also lets between two and seven friends or family members combine their balances, although members must contribute all of their points to the pool while participating.

Related: How to change or cancel a JetBlue flight

JetBlue isn't part of a global alliance, but TrueBlue members can earn and redeem points with the following airline partners.

JetBlue says earning and redeeming with Cape Air are temporarily unavailable while it updates its systems.

Blue Sky lets TrueBlue members earn points and Tiles on eligible United-operated flights booked through JetBlue and redeem TrueBlue points for United flights through JetBlue. Mosaic members also receive reciprocal perks on United, including priority boarding, one complimentary checked bag, preferred seating and Economy Plus seats at check-in. Base fares receive the above benefits except seat selection, and the partnership does not provide reciprocal lounge access.

You can join TrueBlue for free online, starting at the “basic” level. The four published tiers of JetBlue elite status are:

JetBlue uses Tiles to track progress toward "Perks You Pick" — a selection of benefits you can choose from after earning a set number of Tiles — and Mosaic status. You earn 1 Tile for every:

Government-imposed taxes, government-imposed fees and travel insurance do not earn Tiles. Tiles are a status metric and cannot be redeemed for travel.

This means you could earn elite status entirely through credit card spending, through qualifying travel spending or with a combination of the two.

Before reaching Mosaic 1, members can choose a different Perks You Pick benefit at 10, 20, 30 and 40 Tiles. Through Jan. 31, 2027, the choices include early boarding, priority security, a complimentary first inflight alcoholic drink, double points per dollar spent on a JetBlue Vacations package or 5,000 bonus points.

You can pick each of these only once, even if you earn all four Tile amounts.

Related: JetBlue changes its boarding order with new groups

Mosaic members also choose one Perks You Pick benefit at each status level. Current choices include a pet fee waiver, IHG One Rewards Platinum Elite status, Mint Suite selection priority, FoundersCard Blue membership, a $99 statement credit for an eligible JetBlue credit card, a 20-Tile bonus for the member or another TrueBlue member and 15,000 bonus points.

Changes are coming in 2027: Beginning Feb. 1, members will receive a new tier-specific Perks You Pick menu at each Mosaic milestone, may select the same perk again at a later milestone and will have 60 days to make each choice. A pet fee waiver will become an automatic Mosaic 2 benefit, while eligible JetBlue Premier Card members will gain additional card-exclusive choices.

The information for the JetBlue Premier Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Separately, when BlueFirst service begins Dec. 8, all Mosaic members and one companion on the same reservation will be eligible for complimentary, space-available upgrades on eligible BlueFirst flights. Main Base and EvenMore Base fares will not be eligible.

Related: JetBlue announces first-class upgrades and new elite benefits for 2027

There are many ways to save up for a JetBlue award ticket.

When flying JetBlue, you’ll earn TrueBlue points based on the ticket cost, the fare type and whether you book directly with JetBlue.

JetBlue now sells Main, EvenMore, BlueFirst and Mint experiences, with Base and Flex variants available in most cabins. Base fares earn 1 base point per dollar spent, plus 1 point per dollar when booked on jetblue.com or through the JetBlue app. Standard and Flex fares earn 3 base points per dollar spent, plus 3 points per dollar when booked directly.

You can earn TrueBlue points on eligible flights operated by United Airlines, Condor, Etihad Airways, Icelandair, Qatar Airways, Singapore Airlines and South African Airways.

United is different from JetBlue's other partners. TrueBlue members earn 5 points per dollar spent on eligible United-operated flights booked through JetBlue; government-imposed taxes, fees and surcharges are excluded. Eligible United flights credited to TrueBlue also earn Tiles. For most other partners, earning depends on the operating airline, the booking class and the distance flown.

You can find each partner’s earning chart in JetBlue’s partner directory.

There are several ways to earn TrueBlue points without flying:

You can also purchase JetBlue points or pool them with other members.

JetBlue also offers Points On Repeat subscriptions. These provide a set number of TrueBlue points each month. Higher tiers add a flight-earning accelerator, while the top tier also includes a 10% rebate on eligible JetBlue award flights. Compare the subscription cost with the value you expect to receive before enrolling.

JetBlue has four cobranded credit cards, all issued by Barclays:

The information for the JetBlue Premier Card, the JetBlue Plus Card, the JetBlue Card and the JetBlue Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

TrueBlue is also a transfer partner of seven flexible rewards currencies at the following transfer rates:

Related: Credit card transfer partners: Guide to transferring points and miles to airlines and hotels

JetBlue uses a dynamic pricing scheme for its own flights, so redemptions are pretty straightforward. You can redeem points for any seat on any JetBlue-operated flight across its entire route network. The more a flight costs in cash, the more it will cost in points.

According to TPG’s November 2026 valuations, TrueBlue points are worth 1.35 cents each on average. To calculate the value of a specific award, subtract any taxes and fees from the cash price, divide the result by the number of points required and multiply by 100. Mint and Cash + Points bookings may offer less value, while some partner awards can offer more.

To check award availability, search for flights on JetBlue’s website as you normally would and check the “Use TrueBlue points” option at the top of the search box. Base fares can now be booked with points, although JetBlue charges $150 per person to change or cancel a Base award.

Cash + Points bookings start at 500 points and are available for JetBlue-operated flights and eligible JetBlue Vacations packages. This option can be useful if you are short on points, but it often delivers less value than a standard award. Cash + Points bookings are not available for partner airline awards.

TrueBlue points can also cover certain seat assignments, checked bags, pet fees and priority security. You can redeem points through TrueBlue Travel for eligible hotel stays and car rentals as well.

In addition to using your points for JetBlue flights, you can redeem TrueBlue points on JetBlue's site for eligible flights operated by United Airlines, Condor, Etihad Airways, Icelandair, Qatar Airways and China Airlines. Cape Air redemptions are temporarily paused.

Partner award availability can be limited, and each one-way award must be operated by a single carrier. Frustratingly, you cannot combine a JetBlue flight and a partner flight on the same one-way award, although you can book the outbound and return on different airlines.

A Points Pooling account can have two to seven members and must include at least one person age 21 or older. Members contribute 100% of the points they earn after joining. The pool leader and anyone granted redemption privileges can use pooled points without the other members' permission, so only pool with people you trust. A member who leaves takes their remaining points balance with them.

Related: Family points pooling: How to transfer and maximize your rewards

While you’re unlikely to get incredible value from your points, the JetBlue TrueBlue program is still useful for many travelers. TrueBlue points are among the easiest domestic airline points to earn and redeem. JetBlue-operated awards do not require an award chart and have no blackout dates, though partner award availability can be restricted.

JetBlue's expanded partner network makes TrueBlue more globally useful. New transfer partnerships with Rove and Bilt also make it easier to top up a balance. JetBlue's revenue-based pricing usually limits the opportunity for exceptional value on its own flights, but straightforward redemptions and occasional high-value partner awards make TrueBlue worth understanding.

#6057. Capital One Venture Card Bonus: 75K Miles + $300 Credit Welcome Offer (Last Chance)

At the moment, the $95 annual fee Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card is offering a phenomenal limited time welcome bonus, making it the ideal time to apply. I’d like to provide an update that this is the last chance to pick up the card with this offer, as it’s expected to be pulled soon.

Not only is this among the best offers we’ve seen on the card, but this is also a reasonably priced travel rewards card that offers long term value, especially for everyday spending.

Link: Learn more about the Capital One Venture Card

The Capital One Venture Card is currently offering a limited time, lucrative, two-part welcome offer, whereby you can earn 75,000 Capital One bonus miles, plus a $300 Capital One Travel stays credit, after spending $4,000 within the first three months.

For context, Capital One miles can be redeemed for a minimum of one cent each, meaning the 75,000 miles will get you at least $750 in value. However, I value the miles at 1.7 cents each based on my latest analysis (see my methodology here), thanks to the value you can get by transferring the miles to travel partners. That means that to me, the 75,000 miles are worth $1,275.

There are lots of great ways to redeem Capital One miles, as they can be transferred to Capital One’s roughly 20 airline and hotel partners. That’s my preferred use of them, as you can get some amazing travel experiences this way.

Partners include programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue, Qatar Airways Privilege Club, Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, and more. These are all programs that allow you to really maximize your points and get outsized value. Just to give a couple of examples of Capital One mileage redemption opportunities:

That doesn’t include the value of the $300 Capital One Travel credit, which posts upon account approval (rather than upon completing minimum spending). The idea is that this can be used for a hotel or vacation rental booking through Capital One Travel in your first cardmember year (in the first 12 months), and it’s valid across one or multiple stays. In other words, you could use it to pay virtually nothing for a $300 hotel stay. All-in-all, I’d say the Capital One Venture bonus is worth up to $1,575.

By my valuation, the current Capital One Venture Card bonus is the best publicly available offer that we’ve seen in over five years, so that makes this the ideal time to apply, and I absolutely wouldn’t wait for a better offer. Quite to the contrary, when this limited time offer gets pulled, it’ll almost certainly be worse.

For context, below is a history of the publicly available bonuses that we’ve seen on the Capital One Venture in recent years.

As you can see, we’ve never seen a publicly available welcome offer of over 75,000 miles, in terms of the mileage component. We have in the past seen $250 travel credits offered along with the miles, and this time around the travel credit is bigger. So offers really don’t get better than this on the card.

When you look at the bonus terms on the Capital One Venture Card, you’ll find the following language:

You are not eligible for this product if you have received a new cardmember bonus for the Capital One Venture card or the Capital One Venture X card in the past 48 months.

As you can see, the card follows a 48-month rule, so you’re not eligible for the welcome bonus on this card if you’ve received a new cardmember bonus on this exact card or on the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more) in the past 48 months.

Other than that, eligibility is unrelated to having any other credit card, and Capital One doesn’t have many consistent restrictions when it comes to getting approved for cards.

The Capital One Venture Card has a reasonable $95 annual fee, and offers a variety of perks beyond the excellent welcome bonus:

While the Capital One Venture Card is awesome, how does it compare to the Capital One Venture X Card, which is Capital One’s ultra premium credit card? The Venture X has a $395 annual fee, so the fee is significantly higher, but it also offers several great perks that should more than justify the annual fee. Among other things, the Venture X offers:

So when it comes to the Capital One Venture vs. Venture X, personally I think the Venture X is an even better value than the Venture. However, I know some people just want to avoid higher annual fee cards in general, so for those people, the Venture could be a better option.

The limited time Capital One Venture Card bonus currently offers 75,000 Capital One miles plus a $300 Capital One Travel credit upon completing minimum spending. This Capital One Venture bonus is significantly better than usual, so if you’re eligible for the card based on the 48-month bonus rule, I’d absolutely recommend applying. This is the last chance, as the offer is expected to be pulled soon.

Anyone plan to pick up the Capital One Venture Card with this great bonus?

#6056. Delta Holding December 2 Seattle Event To Announce New Singapore Flight—And Pick A Fight With Its Former Partner

Delta Air Lines is throwing an Asian night market in Seattle on December 2, where they’ll finally reveal non-stop Singapore service. That would put Delta into a roughly 17 hour nonstop fight with Singapore Airlines, giving its customers a way to reach one of Asia’s most important business centers without changing planes in Seoul. Enilria reported the December 2 Seattle announcement several days ago and highlighted the invitation’s Asian theme. Aviation watchdog JonNYC has now corroborated that direction, reporting that the event has an “Asian destination inspired holiday night market theme,” then adding: “Singapore as in.” Heard the Delta Seattle event has an Asian destination inspired holiday night market theme — JonNYC (@xJonNYC) November 23, 2026 The invitation is for Delta Night Market at MOPOP, Seattle’s Museum of Pop Culture, on Wednesday, December 2 from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. It promises food, drinks, shopping and cultural experiences built around Asian destinations, along with city-inspired charms guests can collect. The line that caught Enilria’s attention: Seven destinations. One unforgettable night. Delta’s current and announced East and Southeast Asian destinations are Tokyo, Seoul, Shanghai, Taipei, Hong Kong and Manila. That’s seven airports when you count both Tokyo Haneda and Narita, but six cities. If they’re counting cities, Singapore makes seven. So I don’t take this to mean seven new routes, though of course there may be additional routes announced. . And there’s a more concrete clue than the party theme. In a July 29 presentation to a Pacific air traffic coordination group, Delta wrote: New markets announced for 2027 are Manila and Singapore. This Has Been Coming For More Than A Year I reported Delta’s plans to return to Singapore and Manila in October 2025. The following month, I wrote about their internal view that Europe was already pretty full, and that future long haul growth would lean heavily toward Asia, from both Los Angeles and Seattle. JonNYC has been all over this story. In August, Delta revealed at an event for its largest corporate customers that Singapore would follow closely behind Manila. Los Angeles–Manila is scheduled to begin March 28, 2027, initially three times weekly before going daily June 7. Delta last served Singapore in September 2019, as a flight from Tokyo Narita. They dismantled the connecting hub inherited from Northwest, moved their U.S.–Tokyo flying to Haneda and relied more heavily on Korean Air’s Seoul hub to get passengers elsewhere in Asia. Singapore Is A Market Delta Needs To Sell Singapore combines regional headquarters, finance, technology and a wealthy local market. For the multinational business traffic Delta wants, it has become more important than Hong Kong. There are now several times as many regional corporate headquarters in Singapore than Hong Kong. Hong Kong remains a major destination for the Greater Bay Area of China, while Singapore is where companies increasingly put the people managing businesses across the region. Plus, even for the China market Singapore increasingly matters. It’s the first stop for Nvidia chips before moving to Malaysia. Men just want to be seen 😂 https://t.co/a32B5SSQlV — Autism Capital 🧩 (@AutismCapital) November 10, 2026 Delta has been pushing Singapore traffic through Seoul on Korean Air. But a Seattle business traveler isn’t going to want that over a nonstop on Singapore Airlines, or for that matter the entire West Coast market is better served with a Singapore Airlines connection through Seattle, San Francisco or Los Angeles. Those choices can affect domestic flying and credit card spending as well. Meanwhile, Seattle is a shorter trip to Singapore than Los Angeles, which helps with fuel burn and payload on an already very long route. And Alaska is becoming a long haul competitor. It has announced Osaka and Tahiti for 2027, taking its announced Seattle intercontinental network to nine destinations, with a goal of at least 15 by 2030. Delta’s recent additions of Rome and Tokyo Narita have gone directly after Alaska. Singapore would give Delta a destination Alaska doesn’t fly itself. Delta has already invested in a Delta One Lounge and more gate access in Seattle. Adding a long business route gives them another way to sell that investment. The Seattle lounge photo below is courtesy of Delta. Heard the Delta Seattle event has an Asian destination inspired holiday night market theme

The invitation is for Delta Night Market at MOPOP, Seattle’s Museum of Pop Culture, on Wednesday, December 2 from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. It promises food, drinks, shopping and cultural experiences built around Asian destinations, along with city-inspired charms guests can collect. Seven destinations. One unforgettable night.

@alanZ – no, the chips seem to go to malaysia first or to operate as an offshore data center for chinese labs

>>> “DL is following through on focusing its entire growth efforts on Asia/Pacific”

Big mistake if you’re right – putting their “entire” growth in one place. Meanwhile, if they do that, Delta’s competitors will put growth into Asia, AND Europe, AND South America. This is Delta’s problem. They can’t grow and defend everywhere.

They are behind the curve with orders for new planes, while they fly the oldest average aged fleet of all major US carriers (14.9 years, according to planespotters), including 56 767s with an average age of 28.3 years old and in desperate need of replacement.

There’s only so much Pacific growth Delta can do with this widebody delivery timeline:

2027: 8 A350-1000s 2028: 10 A350-1000s 2029: A350-900s (some of 15 start), A330-900neo (some of 16 start) 2030: (probably receive remainder of A350-900 and A330-900neo orders) 2031: 787-10 (first of 30 orders – so, maybe 10?) 3032: Maybe next 10 787-10s? 3033: Maybe final 10 787-10s?

Only American is worse off, as they are considering a new order – and will presumably have to wait even longer to see any new jets if they place one. They are only getting their remaining 19 787s in 2027 and 2028.

United, of course, is receiving the most widebodies the soonest- roughly 140 within the next 4-5 years, compared to Delta’s +/- 55 and American’s 19 over the same period.

That’s the problem with some of the “Here’s what Delta can do against the competition!” predictions. Those predictions are being based on what Delta will do IN THE FUTURE vs. what the competition is doing NOW. It’s easy to see the flaw in that type of analysis.

Instead, if those 140 widebodies for United replace existing planes, you’ve soon have new 787s vs old 767-300s. Easy to guess which will appeal to customers more. If they don’t replace existing planes, you’ll have growth nobody can match – growth that might giving multiple, convenient options to popular destinations, or a route network to locations nobody else can offer. Or most likely both.

United’s bet to place a big order coming out of the pandemic sure looks like it will pay off well for them.

#6055. Delta Plans Seattle To Singapore A350 Flights, Carrier’s Third Longest Route

We know that Delta has huge growth aspirations across the Pacific, particularly to Asia. It’s an area where Delta has increasingly fallen behind United in recent years, but Delta now hopes to not only catch up, but even beat United. We’ll see what comes of that, and in particular, find out just how costly that growth is.

A few months ago, Delta executives publicly confirmed plans to return to Singapore, a destination that hasn’t been served by the airline since 2019, when that was an intra-Asia tag flight from Japan. Executives also confirmed out of which airport the service would operate. There’s now an additional update, as an announcement about the new route is imminent, which almost certainly points to a fall 2027 launch for the service.

As Delta executives view it, the airline is pretty maxed out in terms of its European potential, and in the long run, they see the most long haul growth potential in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa. So, what kind of expansion should we expect?

Back in August 2026, Delta Chief Commercial Officer Joe Esposito explicitly confirmed that the airline would return to Singapore. What was perhaps most interesting is that he also indirectly confirmed the hub out of which the service would operate — Esposito ruled out that the service could operate out of Los Angeles, so it’s pretty clear that the airline will operate this service out of Seattle (SEA).

That’s also what JonNYC reported in the past, and now we can take that a step further — Delta is holding an event in Seattle in early December 2026, and that’s when the airline is expected to announce the service.

My guess is that we’re looking at a fall 2027 service start, at best. At 8,070 miles, this will be Delta’s third longest flight, after its routes to South Africa, which are from Atlanta (ATL) to Cape Town (CPT) and Johannesburg (JNB).

One certainly wonders if this Singapore route could be operated by Delta’s new Airbus A350-1000s, which will feature an all-new passenger experience. While the plane has great range and per seat economics, the only thing I’d say is that it’s “a lot of plane” for a new market, in terms of the overall capacity (even with the very premium layout).

In both the Seattle and Los Angeles to Singapore market, Singapore Airlines is the only other carrier operating. So competitively there’s not a huge difference in that regard, though Los Angeles is a significantly larger market in terms of demand for Singapore, and for that matter, Singapore Airlines also has more service out of the airport. But perhaps Delta is also looking to beat Alaska to the punch in the Seattle market.

It’s fantastic to see Delta looking to grow its presence in Asia. Point-to-point flying to Asia is a market that United has basically had cornered in recent years, and competition is good for consumers.

It’s amazing to think for how many years Delta basically squandered its Asia advantage. Keep in mind that back in the day, Northwest had a robust Asia network, and after the merger with Delta, we saw that network decreased slowly but steadily, as Delta instead focused on routing everything through Seoul Incheon, and into the Korean Air network. So I’m happy to see a reversal of that strategy.

I also have to say that given Delta’s hubris, it’s kind of fun to see the airline having to increasingly play “catch up,” rather than coming in as the dominant carrier. And I think that very much sums up what’s going on in Asia.

The most basic structural disadvantage that Delta has is that United has a fortress hub in San Francisco (SFO), which is where a large part of its Asia network flies from. That’s fantastic for connectivity, not to mention San Francisco is a very strong market for Asia traffic.

Delta, meanwhile, is taking a split hub approach, flying out of both Los Angeles and Seattle. Obviously Delta is trying to make the best of its situation, but there’s no denying that this is an uphill battle:

It also has to be emphasized that in terms of actually transporting passengers profitably (or at less of a loss), United does a better job at that than Delta, despite its lower overall profitability. Comparing passenger revenue per air seat mile to cost per air seat mile, United is at 16.18 cents vs. 16.46 cents, while Delta is at 17.37 cents vs. 19.31 cents.

Delta is growing quite a bit in Asia at the moment. The airline has already launched flights to Hong Kong, with flights now on sale to Manila and Tokyo Narita. On top of that, Delta is expected to announce a new Seattle to Singapore route within the next two weeks, with a launch likely planned for the fall of 2027.

It’s great for passengers to see more competition across the Pacific, as Delta sure is making up for a lack of effort for years. However, the airline will also have quite the disadvantage compared to United for a long time…

What do you make of Delta’s plans to fly to Singapore?

#6054. Tempers flare as future of Social Security debated

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday showed how poisonous the politics could become.

Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

“I think it’s outrageous,” said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking important.”

Johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

"This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he said on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”

But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”

In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson said Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”

Johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he said.

There is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson said Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a plan in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

Senators on both sides of the aisle said they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

“I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability issue, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” said Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.

#6053. Buy Virgin Atlantic Flying Club Points With 80% Bonus (1.1 Cents Each): Worth It?

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is currently offering a best-ever promotion on purchased points. Through December 31, 2026, Flying Club members can purchase points with up to an 80% bonus, which is potentially an opportunity to buy points for under 1.1 cents each. Suffice it to say that this could be a very attractive deal.

Link: Buy Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points with a bonus

Between 12AM GMT on November 24 and 11:59PM GMT on December 31, 2026, the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club program is offering a bonus on purchased points. Virgin Atlantic is offering a tiered bonus of up to 80%, as follows:

Note that the purchase of Virgin Atlantic points is non-refundable, and purchasing points doesn’t count toward Flying Club elite status. Points will be credited to accounts within 24 hours, though they typically post faster than that, and almost instantly.

The cost to purchase Virgin Atlantic points varies based on where your account is registered:

The pricing is much better for those with accounts registered in the UK rather than the US. Assuming you’re eligible for an 80% bonus:

So as you can see, in the United States you can potentially pay 1.39 cents per point, while in the UK you can potentially pay 1.09 cents per point.

It’s interesting how much Virgin Atlantic penalizes those in the United States when it comes to buying points. Then again, when it comes to overall points earning opportunities, we can’t really complain in the United States, given the amazing credit card offers we have.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club ordinarily lets members purchase up to 200,000 points per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been doubled, to 400,000 points.

When Virgin Atlantic Flying Club offers a promotion on purchased points, the best version of the offer is almost always for a 70% bonus. As you can tell, this offer is even better than those, as this is truly a best-ever offer. Personally, I’d recommend buying points based on when you have a short term use in mind, rather than based on the slight difference in the cost per point.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the Flying Club program, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Flying Club points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach minimum spending, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

Virgin Atlantic is definitely a frequent flyer program with more niche redemption opportunities. In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic, there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, and Delta.

Nowadays Virgin Atlantic has dynamic award pricing for its own flights, and for those with flexibility who want the best deal, this can make for some great deals. For example, there are some transatlantic one-way business class awards that cost under 30,000 points, which is amazing.

Beyond that, Virgin Atlantic has several airline partners, some of which are more lucrative than others. Probably the best use of Flying Club points is for travel in ANA first & business class. You can find the redemption rates below.

Paying 52,500-60,000 Flying Club points for a one-way business class ticket between the United States and Japan is a phenomenal value to start with.

All Nippon Airways’ new first & business class are amazing products as well. The major catch is that availability can be really tough to come by.

Everyone will value points currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Flying Club points to be worth 1.1 cents each. However, I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get way more value from Flying Club points than that.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points don’t expire. There’s no requirement to even have any account activity, as the points will never expire regardless.

While buying Virgin Atlantic points could represent a great deal, keep in mind that there are lots of other ways to earn Flying Club points. Most significantly, Virgin Atlantic is partners with major transferable points currencies, including American Express Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, Chase Ultimate Rewards, and Citi ThankYou, and in all cases, points can be moved at a 1:1 ratio. There are several ways to earn these points aside from outright buying them.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is offering members an 80% bonus on purchased points, which is an opportunity to buy points for 1.09-1.39 cents each (in USD), depending on where your account is registered.

There are plenty of circumstances where this could be a great deal. The only major consideration is that there are lots of other ways to earn Virgin Atlantic points with transferable points currencies, so some may prefer to earn rewards that way. With a specific use in mind, there could definitely be huge value in buying Flying Club points.

#6052. Joe Biden Flew Cape Air For Thanksgiving—His Airport Cart Ride Turned Into A Political Fight

Joe Biden carried his bag through Philadelphia airport, got onto a police cart, and wound up at the center of another argument about the 2024 election. Biden and his wife Jill were headed to Nantucket for Thanksgiving. The final leg of the trip was on Cape Air. The former president turned 84 on Friday. He’s dealing with cancer. And he’s still traveling commercially with his wife, albeit with a security detail and a little more help getting through the terminal than most passengers receive. Shakiah Davis posted this video with the caption, “Ran into Joe and his wife today at the PHL…..” Biden walks slowly, carrying a tan leather duffel, then takes a seat on a Philadelphia Police electric cart. Jill is seated on another cart. Here’s the version without the political argument pasted over the footage: View Shakiah Davis’s video of Joe and Jill Biden at Philadelphia airport The Carry On store visible behind Biden is at the top of Philadelphia’s B concourse, next to Passyunk Steaks. This is familiar territory for American Airlines passengers. The Bidens arrived on Nantucket Sunday evening, November 22, on Cape Air from Boston. That was their arrival airline last Thanksgiving, too. Their family tradition of spending the holiday on the island dates to 1975, and they’re staying again at David Rubenstein’s waterfront property. View Nantucket Current’s video of the Bidens’ Thanksgiving arrival Earlier this month he explained why he was cutting back appearances for his new book: Some days are better than others. It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down. The version of the airport video reposted by Western Journal uses it to revisit claims that Biden could have handled another four years in office. The comments on the cleaner version include “Yeah, he could’ve served another 4 years” and Nick Shirley’s “Put him back in office he’s ready for another 4.” But “The guy is fighting cancer………” had more than 23,000 likes when I checked, substantially more than either of those comments. Even under the political repost, one response was, “Not a fan but will pray for him and his family.” I’ve long viewed Biden as an honorable man and a poor president. He let his administration operate like a feudal system, with interest groups controlling their policy areas. That made for bad policy and bad politics, pulling him away from the median voters who elected him. He also wasn’t up to another term. Pretending otherwise delayed a real process to choose his successor, and handing the nomination to Kamala Harris left his party poorly positioned for the election. She was a terrible candidate. But the debate made the problem clear, and he dropped out. A video of him taking an airport cart more than two years doesn’t tell us anything new. Now he’s an airline passenger going to see his family. In June 2025 he was flying United Airlines first class out of Houston. That December he was boarding American Airlines in Miami for St. Croix, standing in the boarding line with an escort. We could enjoy Jimmy Carter walking through a Delta Air Lines cabin and greeting passengers without agreeing about his presidency. Jimmy Carter greeting passengers aboard Delta Air Lines, June 8, 2017 George W. Bush gets more room to be a retired president, too (sometimes more from Democrats than from Trump Republicans, given the split between Trump and the Bush family). Enjoying an encounter with a former president doesn’t require revising your assessment of his time in office. There are still airline issues worth arguing about. In June 2025, I criticized American Airlines bumping a passenger from first class to accommodate Biden on flight 2717 from Minneapolis to Philadelphia. He’d been attending the funeral of murdered Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman. A former president’s scheduling preferences shouldn’t outrank someone else’s confirmed seat. If the airline needs room for his party, it can ask for volunteers and pay them enough to take a different seat or flight. It seems President Trump, who already owned aircraft before entering office, may have an ex-Qatari royal 747 at his disposal. Hopefully better judgment will prevail there. BushHand luggageHoustonJimmy CarterKamala HarrisMiamiMinneapolisMinnesotaNantucketPhiladelphiaPhiladelphia International AirportQatarSaint CroixUnited Airlines+19 more More From View from the Wing

The former president turned 84 on Friday. He’s dealing with cancer. And he’s still traveling commercially with his wife, albeit with a security detail and a little more help getting through the terminal than most passengers receive.

Shakiah Davis posted this video with the caption, “Ran into Joe and his wife today at the PHL…..” Biden walks slowly, carrying a tan leather duffel, then takes a seat on a Philadelphia Police electric cart. Jill is seated on another cart. Here’s the version without the political argument pasted over the footage:

View Shakiah Davis’s video of Joe and Jill Biden at Philadelphia airport

The Carry On store visible behind Biden is at the top of Philadelphia’s B concourse, next to Passyunk Steaks. This is familiar territory for American Airlines passengers. The Bidens arrived on Nantucket Sunday evening, November 22, on Cape Air from Boston. That was their arrival airline last Thanksgiving, too. Their family tradition of spending the holiday on the island dates to 1975, and they’re staying again at David Rubenstein’s waterfront property.

View Nantucket Current’s video of the Bidens’ Thanksgiving arrival

Earlier this month he explained why he was cutting back appearances for his new book:

Some days are better than others. It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down.

The version of the airport video reposted by Western Journal uses it to revisit claims that Biden could have handled another four years in office. The comments on the cleaner version include “Yeah, he could’ve served another 4 years” and Nick Shirley’s “Put him back in office he’s ready for another 4.”

But “The guy is fighting cancer………” had more than 23,000 likes when I checked, substantially more than either of those comments. Even under the political repost, one response was, “Not a fan but will pray for him and his family.”

I’ve long viewed Biden as an honorable man and a poor president. He let his administration operate like a feudal system, with interest groups controlling their policy areas. That made for bad policy and bad politics, pulling him away from the median voters who elected him.

He also wasn’t up to another term. Pretending otherwise delayed a real process to choose his successor, and handing the nomination to Kamala Harris left his party poorly positioned for the election. She was a terrible candidate. But the debate made the problem clear, and he dropped out. A video of him taking an airport cart more than two years doesn’t tell us anything new. Now he’s an airline passenger going to see his family.

In June 2025 he was flying United Airlines first class out of Houston. That December he was boarding American Airlines in Miami for St. Croix, standing in the boarding line with an escort.

We could enjoy Jimmy Carter walking through a Delta Air Lines cabin and greeting passengers without agreeing about his presidency.

Jimmy Carter greeting passengers aboard Delta Air Lines, June 8, 2017

George W. Bush gets more room to be a retired president, too (sometimes more from Democrats than from Trump Republicans, given the split between Trump and the Bush family). Enjoying an encounter with a former president doesn’t require revising your assessment of his time in office.

There are still airline issues worth arguing about. In June 2025, I criticized American Airlines bumping a passenger from first class to accommodate Biden on flight 2717 from Minneapolis to Philadelphia. He’d been attending the funeral of murdered Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman.

A former president’s scheduling preferences shouldn’t outrank someone else’s confirmed seat. If the airline needs room for his party, it can ask for volunteers and pay them enough to take a different seat or flight. It seems President Trump, who already owned aircraft before entering office, may have an ex-Qatari royal 747 at his disposal. Hopefully better judgment will prevail there.

One of the top premium cards, the offers many lifestyle-centered benefits and statement credits. Those include several health- and fitness-centered benefits, including an Oura Ring statement credit for up to $200 per calendar year (enrollment is required).

With the end of the calendar year fast approaching, now's a good time to decide whether you can use this credit before it resets.

Here's how this statement credit works and whether it makes sense for you.

One of the many lifestyle statement credits available through the is up to $200 each calendar year toward Oura Ring. Specifically, the statement credit applies to hardware purchases only and doesn't cover subscriptions. (Enrollment is required.)

The Oura Ring is a wearable, health-tracking smart ring. Some key data it tracks includes:

Imagine an Apple Watch or Fitbit, but in ring form. Oura currently sells the Oura Ring 4 starting at $349 and the newer Oura Ring 5 starting at $399. While this statement credit won't fully cover the cost of a ring, it will get you more than halfway there.

One notable advantage of the Oura Ring is that you don't have to charge it as often as other wearables — the Oura Ring 5 typically lasts six or more days on a full charge.

Related: The best credit cards to maximize fitness spending

Amex states that the statement credit should post within eight weeks, but some TPG staffers have seen it post within days.

If you're trying to use this statement credit before Dec. 31, don't wait for the last minute. Amex relies on the date Oura processes the transaction, which might be a day or two after you place the order.

This is particularly important if you order a sizing kit: The ring itself won't process and ship until you confirm your size in your Oura account. Place your order now to get things started.

Related: Why the new Amex Platinum changes are converting me to a cardmember

This statement credit is a more niche perk that not all cardmembers will be able to use. For starters, many people may prefer other forms of wearables. If health data doesn't interest you, this statement credit won't move the needle either.

Plus, the fact that this statement credit doesn't cover the full cost of the ring may also deter some cardmembers. The out-of-pocket cost will still run you at least $149, unless you land a good sale. You'll also need to pay for an Oura Membership at $5.99 monthly or $69.99 per year.

I hope Amex expands this statement credit to cover a subscription in the future, since it's needed to fully maximize your Oura Ring's features.

Even if Oura Ring is of interest, you may not want to buy a new one every year, meaning some years the benefit may go unused.

If you don't think you’d use the statement credit yourself, you could gift a ring to one of your health- and fitness-minded friends or family members.

It's also important to note that this is a shared statement credit, meaning authorized users do not receive their own.

This sole statement credit shouldn't be the deciding factor on whether you add this card to your wallet, but if you can use it organically, it can help recoup some of the Platinum's $895 annual fee (see rates and fees).

Related: Complete guide to authorized users on the Amex Platinum Card

The Oura Ring statement credit can be valuable for Platinum Card members who already plan to buy a fitness tracker, especially if they can stack it with a sale. However, you might find it smarter to let the statement credit go unused some or all years.

However, it would be ideal if this statement credit were expanded in the future to cover the subscription cost, as this would make it more accessible for more cardmembers to use year after year.

#6050. Island Mayor Pleads With Japan Airlines Mileage Runners After Locals Can’t Book Flights

The concept of mileage running is making headlines in Japan, and not in a good way. A lucrative promotion from Japan Airlines reportedly caused passengers to take up to 12 flights per day in remote markets, in some cases making it difficult for locals to book flights. What a story this is!

News On Japan has the story of how mileage running has caused issues for locals on some of Okinawa’s remote islands, as they’ve struggled to purchase Japan Airlines tickets due to a flood of mileage runners.

While the story has been published in recent days, it seems to date back to February 2026 (best I can tell), when Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank program was offering double Life Status Points for flights. This promotion incentivized all domestic flights equally, so some savvy frequent flyers decided to seek out the shortest flights, so that they could cram in as many flights in a day as possible.

This ended up bringing them to Okinawa, where you’ll find some of the shortest flights in Japan Airlines’ system. These include flights between Ishigaki (ISG), Miyako (MMY), Naha (OKA), and Tarama (TRA). According to reports, some mileage runners booked up to a staggering 12 flights per day, leaving few empty seats on some essential flights.

At Miyako Airport, some passengers were observed arriving with just small handbags, and then immediately heading to the departures area to board their next flight. As a few travelers explained:

The issue is that this mileage running reportedly created serious difficulties for locals, who depend on the island flights for medical appointments, shopping, and other essential travel. There were some successive days in February where flights between Miyako and Tarama were booked out in advance, leaving locals unable to book seats. Here’s what some locals had to say:

Tarama Mayor Mitsuo Iranami even called on mileage runners to consider the impact their activities were having on the island community, commenting “I would like those doing mileage runs to understand the situation on remote islands and exercise some consideration, taking into account the number of people participating.”

Japan Airlines reportedly even introduced measures intended to counteract this, including offering full refunds without cancellation fees, along with 500 bonus miles as an incentive. Below is a news story in Japanese about this, so you can watch that with subtitles, if you’d like.

I think this story is a good reminder of just how well frequent flyer programs can work with the purpose of filling seats on planes… for better or worse!

While it’s fairly common to see loyalty programs offer promotions, nowadays it’s rare to see deals that are actually that lucrative. When it does happen, we sometimes see that the people behind the promotion clearly didn’t think through all possible scenarios, and this is one of those situations.

While Japan Airlines’ double status points promotion in February is pretty standard, the airline has added a new restriction for the offer this coming year, by capping the number of bonus points that can be earned during the promotion period, presumably to prevent something like this from happening.

Obviously I feel bad for the locals in this situation, but it’s also hard to blame frequent flyers here for simply taking advantage of a promotion as advertised.

Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank frequent flyer program ran a promotion that might have just done too good of a job getting people to book flights, as a double Life Status Points offer caused some people to book up to a dozen flights per day, with some flights reportedly having up to 80% of passengers be mileage runners.

Ordinarily that would be considered a success in terms of filling planes, but the issue here is that mileage runners descended on island routes that are also a lifeline for residents, given the efficiency of flying there. It’s not often you hear a mayor make a plea with mileage runners, but that’s exactly what happened here.

What do you make of this Japan Airlines mileage run promotion situation?

#6049. Thrifty Traveler Is 30% Off For Black Friday—A Year Of Flight And Business Class Award Alerts For $90.99

They tell me this is their biggest sale of the year, and the biggest they expect to offer for the foreseeable future. It matches the 30% discount I covered in August.

Readers who took advantage of the offer before their March price increase did better: $79 for the first year and $99 for renewals. That offer’s gone. The regular annual prices are now $129.99 and $189.99, and their price lock guarantee applies to those full prices, not the discounted first year.

I’ve said this is one of the better services for finding rare premium cabin awards. They search departures from more than 200 airports in the U.S. and Canada, and you choose which airports you want alerts for. You can stick to your home airport or include other cities you’re willing to position to.

Deals arrive by email, there’s an online hub where you can browse them, and you can opt into text alerts for mistake fares and their rarest “unicorn” deals. They say they’ve recently sent more than 80 flight alerts in a month, including more than 30 business class award alerts, such as:

Most alerts won’t fit any one person’s plans. I like this most for someone with transferable points who can let award availability help decide where to go. Finding one useful business class award can easily justify the subscription. If you need a particular flight on a particular date, though, a stream of deals to other places isn’t going to solve that.

They’ve also added FareTracker. Premium members can track up to 10 cash flights and get an email when the price drops by at least $20, with instructions to rebook and claim the difference as an airline credit. You still need a fare whose rules allow that, and you have to do the rebooking. But it’s a useful reason to keep watching a ticket after you’ve bought it.

The Premium+ bundle adds hotel deals, including difficult award availability and discounted paid stays. Recent alerts have included Park Hyatt Kyoto and the renovated Waldorf Astoria New York. The extra $42 makes sense if you’d build a trip around finding award nights at a property like that.

#6048. Flydubai Resuming Israel Flights After Pilot Tried To Crash Plane Into Airport

On September 30, 2026, we saw an unbelievably horrifying attempted terror plot, whereby a flydubai Boeing 737 first officer attempted to hijack the plane he was second in command of, and crash it into Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport.

He attempted to kill the captain of the flight using the axe in the cockpit, but thank goodness the captain managed to open the door after being struck, so that passengers could restrain the first officer. The details that have come out ever since have been downright chilling, including how the Omani pilot had specifically sought out a job at flydubai because the airline flew to Israel, and he wanted to crash into the airport there.

Ever since that incident, flydubai has been banned from flying to Israel. For that matter, air service between Israel and the United Arab Emirates is just a tiny fraction of what it previously was. However, there’s now an update, and it looks like this service could resume very soon.

The Times of Israel reports that Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev has approved the resumption of flydubai flights to Israel, pending approval from Israel’s security authorities.

This approval comes after a delegation of Israeli security and transportation officials traveled to Dubai to meet with their counterparts, to discuss new security measures to allow airlines to resume flights between Tel Aviv and Dubai.

Emirati officials reportedly presented the Israeli officials with new steps that have been taken to ensure security in light of the incident, but details beyond that haven’t been made public. Per a statement from the Israeli Transportation Ministry:

“The delegation today presented Regev with the steps the company has taken in the wake of the incident. As a result, Regev approved the return of flydubai, subject to clearance from security authorities. The move is a significant step toward restoring air connectivity between Israel and the UAE and expanding flight options for passengers.”

Tel Aviv was flydubai’s single biggest destination, as the airline operated in the market with up to 10 daily flights. Previously, Israeli authorities had banned flydubai from returning to the country through at least December 15, 2026.

Let's talk about that missing rudder of Flydubai 1073 B737 MAX 8.The aerodynamic forces involved may have been large enough to cause rudder failure through aerodynamic flutter during the extreme overspeed.The aircraft descended more than 14,000 ft in under 30 seconds.Even… pic.twitter.com/ECA34H4IXG

Israel is typically known for its very tight security and good intelligence, but obviously there are lapses sometimes.

One of the odd things about the flydubai attempted terror attack is that the Israeli government reportedly had a policy whereby pilots of foreign airlines couldn’t hold citizenship with countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with Israel. Oman and Israel don’t have diplomatic relations, so based on that, the first officer shouldn’t have been able to fly on the plane.

However, it sure seems that there wasn’t actually enforcement of this rule, given that the flydubai first officer had flown to Tel Aviv several times before. I’d imagine that Israeli forces will now much more closely screen the pilots on these flights.

I am curious if there were some new policies put in place beyond that, or if the extent of the enforcement here is that it’s about the potential nationality of pilots.

Israeli authorities have met with their counterparts in the UAE, and the plan is for flydubai to be able to resume flights to Israel in the near future. This comes nearly two months after the awful terror plot, whereby a flydubai pilot intended to kill the captain, and then fly a 737 full of passengers into the terminal at Ben Gurion Airport.

Some new security policies have reportedly been put into place, though the details of that aren’t being made public. I think one thing is for sure — Israeli authorities will carefully be scrutinizing manifests and keeping an eye on the pilots at the controls of these flights.

This resumption is a big deal for flydubai, given that Tel Aviv was the carrier’s biggest market.

What do you make of flydubai resuming Israel flights?

#6046. Fascinating Air Saint-Pierre Domestic Transatlantic Flight Returns In 2027

One of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027. Maybe this will be the year I finally get to try it, even if there’s no premium cabin angle!

In the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route launched — it operated seasonally once weekly. Specifically, ASL Airlines operated a Boeing 737-700 that was marketed by Air Saint-Pierre between Paris (CDG) and Saint Pierre and Miquelon (FSP).

What’s Saint Pierre and Miquelon? It’s a self-governing territory of France, situated in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean, near Newfoundland and Labrador. The islands cover an area of about 93 square miles, and have a population of just about 6,000 people.

The territory’s airline, Air Saint-Pierre, only has turboprops, which the carrier flies to places like Halifax (YHZ), Montreal (YUL), and St. John’s (YYT). Obviously these planes aren’t capable of operating across the Atlantic, so the airline leases a Boeing 737 for the once weekly flight.

This was the first time ever that we saw a nonstop link between these territories and mainland France. There were some other things that made this route interesting:

The route ended up returning in 2019, was then paused in 2020 and 2021 due to the pandemic, and then returned in 2022 through 2026. The route will now be returning yet again, for the 2027 season, so it sure seems like this is basically a permanent thing.

The once weekly flight between Saint Pierre and Miquelon and Paris will be returning in 2027, between June 21 and September 6, 2027.

The route will once again be operated by an ASL Airlines France Boeing 737-700, and the flight will be marketed and sold by Air Saint-Pierre. The flight will operate westbound on Mondays and eastbound on Tuesdays, as follows:

Paris to Saint Pierre and Miquelon departing 4:00PM arriving 6:30PMSaint Pierre and Miquelon to Paris departing 10:30AM arriving 8:05PM

The 2,664-mile flight is blocked at 6hr30min westbound and 5hr35min eastbound. As you can see, the plane sits on the ground in Saint Pierre for quite a while. This is so that the crew can get their rest and operate the flight back the next day, rather than making them stay there for over a week.

I imagine the airline is able to get a decent deal on parking at the airport for 16 hours. 😉 It’s also interesting since this is an eastbound daytime transatlantic flight, which is fairly rare.

If you want to book a seat on this flight, below is the pricing for travel in both directions, with fares starting at €660 one-way for standard adult fares.

As you can see, the fare difference just comes down to the age of the traveler, as well as the level of flexibility you’d like, with fares either being non-refundable and non-changeable, non-refundable but changeable for a fee, or refundable and changeable. The plane is in an all-economy configuration, as there’s no premium cabin.

Air Saint-Pierre will be bringing back its flight between Saint Pierre and Paris in the summer of 2027, operated by ASL Airlines. This is an absolutely fascinating route, and it’s so cool to see that it was launched in the first place, and is sticking around.

While the link between Paris and this French territory is obvious, it’s still kind of awesome that such a small territory can support a flight like this. But I guess the downside was fairly limited, since the route was subsidized from the beginning. Personally I find this to be the most intriguing transatlantic route.

Anyone else love this Air Saint-Pierre flight as much as I do?
